claim: Over 40% of the world population is at risk of dengue infection.
source: Over 40% of the world population is at risk of dengue infection.
evidence: This is a statement about global dengue risk that is presented as established fact in the introduction.

claim: An estimated 105 million infections and approximately 50 million symptomatic cases occur each year.
source: An estimated 105 million infections and approximately 50 million symptomatic cases occur each year (Stanaway et al., 2016; Cattarino et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dengue disease is caused by four distinct viruses, termed serotypes (DENV-1–4).
source: Dengue disease is caused by four distinct viruses, termed serotypes (DENV- 1–4).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about dengue virus classification.

claim: Infection confers lifelong immunity to a homologous serotype.
source: Infection confers lifelong immunity to a homologous serotype, but against a heterologous serotype protective immunity is only temporary (St John and Rathore, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Against a heterologous serotype protective immunity is only temporary.
source: Infection confers lifelong immunity to a homologous serotype, but against a heterologous serotype protective immunity is only temporary (St John and Rathore, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Secondary infection with a heterologous serotype drastically increases the likelihood of disease.
source: Furthermore, secondary infection with a heterologous serotype drastically increases the likelihood of disease (St John and Rathore, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Traditional vector control interventions have had little impact on dengue disease burden.
source: Traditional vector control interventions have had little impact on dengue disease burden (Guzman et al., 2010) and no antiviral treatments yet exist.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: No antiviral treatments yet exist for dengue.
source: Traditional vector control interventions have had little impact on dengue disease burden (Guzman et al., 2010) and no antiviral treatments yet exist.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the current state of dengue treatment.

claim: The only licensed dengue vaccine is Sanofi-Pasteur's CYD-TDV (marketed as Dengvaxia).
source: Several vaccine candidates are in development, but the only licensed vaccine is Sanofi-Pasteur's CYD-TDV (marketed as Dengvaxia).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the current regulatory status of dengue vaccines.

claim: CYD-TDV is a live attenuated tetravalent chimeric vaccine.
source: CYD-TDV is a live attenuated tetravalent chimeric vaccine, where genes for the structural proteins (E and prM) are taken from the four DENV serotypes, while the other proteins are based on the yellow fever 17D vaccine strain.
evidence: This is a description of the vaccine's composition based on established knowledge.

claim: In CYD-TDV, genes for the structural proteins (E and prM) are taken from the four DENV serotypes, while the other proteins are based on the yellow fever 17D vaccine strain.
source: CYD-TDV is a live attenuated tetravalent chimeric vaccine, where genes for the structural proteins (E and prM) are taken from the four DENV serotypes, while the other proteins are based on the yellow fever 17D vaccine strain.
evidence: This is a description of the vaccine's composition based on established knowledge.

claim: The CYD-TDV vaccine has been licensed in 21 countries and the EU.
source: The vaccine has now been licensed in 21 countries and the EU.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the vaccine's regulatory status.

claim: A phase two trial in 2012 reported moderate efficacy of 30.2% (−13.4% to 56.6%).
source: A phase two trial in 2012 (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT00842530) (Sabchareon et al., 2012) reported moderate efficacy of 30.2% (−13.4% to 56.6%) and showed the vaccine to be well tolerated and largely safe.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published trial.

claim: The phase two trial showed the vaccine to be well tolerated and largely safe.
source: A phase two trial in 2012 (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT00842530) (Sabchareon et al., 2012) reported moderate efficacy of 30.2% (−13.4% to 56.6%) and showed the vaccine to be well tolerated and largely safe.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published trial.

claim: The CYD14 trial in South East Asia included 10,275 children aged 2–14.
source: Two large scale phase three trials followed: the CYD14 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01373281) in South East Asia of 10,275 children aged 2–14 (Capeding et al., 2014), and the CYD15 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01374516) in Latin America of 20,869 children aged 9–16 (Villar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published trial reports.

claim: The CYD15 trial in Latin America included 20,869 children aged 9–16.
source: Two large scale phase three trials followed: the CYD14 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01373281) in South East Asia of 10,275 children aged 2–14 (Capeding et al., 2014), and the CYD15 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01374516) in Latin America of 20,869 children aged 9–16 (Villar et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published trial reports.

claim: Participants were randomly assigned to vaccine or control arms in a 2:1 ratio.
source: After stratifying by age, participants were randomly assigned to vaccine or control arms in a 2:1 ratio, and vaccine doses were given at baseline then 6 and 12 months later.
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: Vaccine doses were given at baseline then 6 and 12 months later.
source: After stratifying by age, participants were randomly assigned to vaccine or control arms in a 2:1 ratio, and vaccine doses were given at baseline then 6 and 12 months later.
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: For approximately 20% of CYD14 participants, immunogenicity and prior dengue exposure was determined using baseline sera.
source: For a subset of participants (approximately 20% for CYD14% and 10% for CYD15), immunogenicity and prior dengue exposure was determined using baseline sera.
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: For approximately 10% of CYD15 participants, immunogenicity and prior dengue exposure was determined using baseline sera.
source: For a subset of participants (approximately 20% for CYD14% and 10% for CYD15), immunogenicity and prior dengue exposure was determined using baseline sera.
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: Participants were actively surveilled by weekly phone calls for 25 months post-first dose.
source: Participants were actively surveilled by weekly phone calls for 25 months post-first dose (where any symptomatic disease was detected), after which surveillance was passive using routine hospital surveillance, (where only hospitalisations were detected).
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: During active surveillance, any symptomatic disease was detected.
source: Participants were actively surveilled by weekly phone calls for 25 months post-first dose (where any symptomatic disease was detected), after which surveillance was passive using routine hospital surveillance, (where only hospitalisations were detected).
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: During passive surveillance, only hospitalisations were detected.
source: Participants were actively surveilled by weekly phone calls for 25 months post-first dose (where any symptomatic disease was detected), after which surveillance was passive using routine hospital surveillance, (where only hospitalisations were detected).
evidence: This describes the trial design as reported in the cited publications.

claim: The CYD14 trial showed overall vaccine efficacy of 56.5% (43.8%–66.4%).
source: The CYD14 and CYD15 trials showed overall vaccine efficacies of 56.5% (43.8%–66.4%) and 60.8% (52.0%–68.0%) respectively, with efficacy varying significantly by serotype and prior exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published trial reports.

claim: The CYD15 trial showed overall vaccine efficacy of 60.8% (52.0%–68.0%).
source: The CYD14 and CYD15 trials showed overall vaccine efficacies of 56.5% (43.8%–66.4%) and 60.8% (52.0%–68.0%) respectively, with efficacy varying significantly by serotype and prior exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published trial reports.

claim: Vaccine efficacy varied significantly by serotype and prior exposure.
source: The CYD14 and CYD15 trials showed overall vaccine efficacies of 56.5% (43.8%–66.4%) and 60.8% (52.0%–68.0%) respectively, with efficacy varying significantly by serotype and prior exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published trial reports.

claim: Results from the first year of long-term follow up showed that the number of hospitalisations among 2–5 year olds was significantly greater in vaccinees than in controls.
source: However, in 2015, results from the first year of long-term follow up (Hadinegoro et al., 2015) showed that while the vaccine remained beneficial overall, the number of hospitalisations among 2–5 year olds was significantly greater in vaccinees than in controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published follow-up data.

claim: The vaccine remained beneficial overall during the first year of long-term follow up.
source: However, in 2015, results from the first year of long-term follow up (Hadinegoro et al., 2015) showed that while the vaccine remained beneficial overall, the number of hospitalisations among 2–5 year olds was significantly greater in vaccinees than in controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published follow-up data.

claim: Age may act as a proxy for serostatus in explaining increased hospitalisation risk.
source: A potential explanation for these results considered age as a proxy for serostatus (Aguiar and Stollenwerk, 2018), and that the vaccine may act as a 'silent' disease-free infection that primes host immunity (Ferguson et al., 2016; Flasche et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published analyses.

claim: The vaccine may act as a 'silent' disease-free infection that primes host immunity.
source: A potential explanation for these results considered age as a proxy for serostatus (Aguiar and Stollenwerk, 2018), and that the vaccine may act as a 'silent' disease-free infection that primes host immunity (Ferguson et al., 2016; Flasche et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published analyses.

claim: A seronegative child who would ordinarily experience their first and relatively low-risk natural infection would after vaccination instead experience a 'secondary-like' infection that is more predisposed to clinically apparent disease.
source: Therefore, a seronegative child, who would ordinarily experience their first and relatively low-risk natural infection, would after vaccination instead experience a 'secondary-like' infection that is more predisposed to clinically apparent disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 'silent infection' hypothesis and cited literature.

claim: A child with a single prior natural infection would have a lower risk of disease when exposed to dengue post-vaccination, normally associated with tertiary and quaternary infection.
source: Conversely, a child with a single prior natural infection would have a lower risk of disease when exposed to dengue post-vaccination, normally associated with tertiary and quaternary infection [Figure 1].
evidence: This is an inference based on the 'silent infection' hypothesis and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The immunogenicity subset was only a small fraction of the entire trial.
source: The immunogenicity subset was only a small fraction of the entire trial, and the estimated efficacy in seronegatives had wide confidence intervals indicating neither benefit nor harm, and so it was not possible to determine conclusively whether age or lack of prior exposure was the dominant factor in the increased hospitalisation of 2–5 year-old vaccinees.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the trial data.

claim: The estimated efficacy in seronegatives had wide confidence intervals indicating neither benefit nor harm.
source: The immunogenicity subset was only a small fraction of the entire trial, and the estimated efficacy in seronegatives had wide confidence intervals indicating neither benefit nor harm, and so it was not possible to determine conclusively whether age or lack of prior exposure was the dominant factor in the increased hospitalisation of 2–5 year-old vaccinees.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the trial data analysis.

claim: It was not possible to determine conclusively whether age or lack of prior exposure was the dominant factor in the increased hospitalisation of 2–5 year-old vaccinees.
source: The immunogenicity subset was only a small fraction of the entire trial, and the estimated efficacy in seronegatives had wide confidence intervals indicating neither benefit nor harm, and so it was not possible to determine conclusively whether age or lack of prior exposure was the dominant factor in the increased hospitalisation of 2–5 year-old vaccinees.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the trial data analysis.

claim: It was not possible to retroactively expand the immunogenicity subset to determine prior dengue exposure, as Dengvaxia can elicit antibody responses that would test positive under a plaque reduction neutralisation test (PRNT).
source: Further, it was not possible to retroactively expand the immunogenicity subset to determine prior dengue exposure, as Dengvaxia can elicit antibody responses that would test positive under a plaque reduction neutralisation test (PRNT).
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation of the available testing methods.

claim: The vaccine showed the greatest benefit in children aged nine or older.
source: Therefore, and because the vaccine showed the greatest benefit in children aged nine or older, the vaccine was licensed for use above this age, independent of baseline serostatus.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the trial data that informed licensing decisions.

claim: The vaccine was licensed for use above age nine, independent of baseline serostatus.
source: Therefore, and because the vaccine showed the greatest benefit in children aged nine or older, the vaccine was licensed for use above this age, independent of baseline serostatus.
evidence: This is stated as a regulatory decision based on trial data.

claim: An ELISA assay detecting anti-dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) IgG antibodies provided a novel approach to retrospectively assess the serostatus of trial participants prior to vaccination.
source: An ELISA assay detecting anti-dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) IgG antibodies then provided a novel approach to retrospectively assess the serostatus of trial participants prior to vaccination (Nascimento et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published methodology.

claim: Dengvaxia expresses yellow fever NS1, not dengue NS1.
source: Dengvaxia expresses yellow fever NS1, not dengue NS1, and therefore this assay can distinguish between natural infection and exposure to the vaccine.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the vaccine that enables the NS1 assay to work.

claim: The NS1 assay can distinguish between natural infection and exposure to the vaccine.
source: Dengvaxia expresses yellow fever NS1, not dengue NS1, and therefore this assay can distinguish between natural infection and exposure to the vaccine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the vaccine's properties and the assay's mechanism.

claim: Blood samples of trial participants who contracted virologically confirmed dengue during follow-up were analysed using the NS1 assay in the CYD14 and CYD15 trials.
source: Blood samples of trial participants who contracted virologically confirmed dengue during follow-up were analysed using the NS1 assay in the CYD14 and CYD15 trials.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the retrospective analysis.

claim: The NS1 assay results provided clear evidence of the enhanced risk of hospitalised or severe dengue disease in baseline seronegative vaccinees.
source: The results provided clear evidence of the enhanced risk of hospitalised or severe dengue disease in baseline seronegative vaccinees (Sridhar et al., 2018) and these were in line with refined estimates of vaccine efficacy obtained with machine learning (Dorigatti et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published analyses.

claim: The NS1 assay results were in line with refined estimates of vaccine efficacy obtained with machine learning.
source: The results provided clear evidence of the enhanced risk of hospitalised or severe dengue disease in baseline seronegative vaccinees (Sridhar et al., 2018) and these were in line with refined estimates of vaccine efficacy obtained with machine learning (Dorigatti et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published analyses.

claim: In November 2017, Dengvaxia was recommended only in persons with a confirmed prior dengue infection.
source: Subsequently, in November 2017, Dengvaxia was recommended only in persons with a confirmed prior dengue infection (WHO, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO guidance.

claim: The study fits a survival model to individual-level data from both CYD14 and CYD15 trials, including year 1 of hospital follow-up.
source: Here we present a survival model with time and age varying hazards, which we fit to the individual level phase three CYD14 and CYD15 data, up to and including the first year of long-term follow-up (Hadinegoro et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: The study characterizes the efficacy profile and mode of action of the vaccine.
source: We characterize the efficacy profile and mode of action of the vaccine, which we find to be consistent with the 'vaccine as silent infection' hypothesis.
evidence: This describes the aims and findings of the current study.

claim: The vaccine's mode of action is consistent with the 'vaccine as silent infection' hypothesis.
source: We characterize the efficacy profile and mode of action of the vaccine, which we find to be consistent with the 'vaccine as silent infection' hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling analysis of trial data.

claim: The study examines the vaccine's duration of protection and its efficacy against both febrile dengue disease and hospitalized disease.
source: We refine previous estimates, and examine the vaccine's duration of protection and its efficacy against both febrile dengue disease and hospitalized disease.
evidence: This describes the scope of the current study's analysis.

claim: The results demonstrate the need for long-term follow up in the phase three trials of other dengue vaccine candidates currently in development.
source: Our results provide a comprehensive characterization of CYD-TDV's safety and efficacy, and demonstrate the need for long-term follow up in the phase three trials of other dengue vaccine candidates currently in development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings about CYD-TDV's long-term effects.

claim: Infecting serotype is known for 97.6% of cases in CYD14.
source: Infecting serotype is known for almost all cases (97.6% for CYD14, 95.8% for CYD15, 96.7% overall).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the trial data used in the study.

claim: Infecting serotype is known for 95.8% of cases in CYD15.
source: Infecting serotype is known for almost all cases (97.6% for CYD14, 95.8% for CYD15, 96.7% overall).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the trial data used in the study.

claim: Infecting serotype is known for 96.7% of cases overall.
source: Infecting serotype is known for almost all cases (97.6% for CYD14, 95.8% for CYD15, 96.7% overall).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the trial data used in the study.

claim: Baseline serostatus is known for 19.3% of subjects in CYD14.
source: Baseline serostatus is known for only a minority of subjects (19.3% for CYD14, 9.6% for CYD15, 12.7% overall).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the trial data used in the study.

claim: Baseline serostatus is known for 9.6% of subjects in CYD15.
source: Baseline serostatus is known for only a minority of subjects (19.3% for CYD14, 9.6% for CYD15, 12.7% overall).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the trial data used in the study.

claim: Baseline serostatus is known for 12.7% of subjects overall.

evidence: This describes a characteristic of the trial data used in the study.

claim: The model considers a country-specific baseline hazard of disease as a spline.
source: We consider a country-specific baseline hazard of disease (or force of infection, i.e. the risk of disease among susceptibles) as a spline λc(t), and we link baseline seropositivity to each participant's age and the background transmission intensity in their country (see below).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the modeling approach.

claim: The model links baseline seropositivity to each participant's age and the background transmission intensity in their country.
source: We consider a country-specific baseline hazard of disease (or force of infection, i.e. the risk of disease among susceptibles) as a spline λc(t), and we link baseline seropositivity to each participant's age and the background transmission intensity in their country (see below).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the modeling approach.

claim: The model assumes exponential waning of transient immunity.
source: In all model variants, we allow the initial magnitude and mean duration of transient immunity to vary by baseline serostatus (exponential waning is assumed).
evidence: This describes a methodological assumption in the modeling approach, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model allows transient immunity magnitude to vary by age and serotype, as well as baseline serostatus.
source: Our main model allows transient immunity magnitude to vary by age and serotype, as well as baseline serostatus.
evidence: This describes the main model structure, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The model incorporates serotype effects additively.
source: For each serostatus, we model transient immunity with age, and serotype effects are incorporated additively (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the modeling approach, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The model includes an age-specific multiplier of the baseline hazard.
source: We further include an age-specific multiplier of the baseline hazard.
evidence: This describes a component of the main model structure, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Both trials show a clear benefit of vaccine across each age group for the active phase.
source: Both trials show a clear benefit of vaccine across each age group for the active phase (25 months post-first dose), where surveillance could detect both hospitalised and non-hospitalised disease.
evidence: This is an observation from the trial data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the passive phase, there are considerably fewer cases than in the active phase, owing to its shorter duration and detection of only hospitalised cases.
source: In the passive phase (next 11 months following active phase), there are considerably fewer cases, owing to its shorter duration and detection of only hospitalised cases.
evidence: This is an observation from the trial data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The benefits of vaccination in the passive phase are less than in the active phase.
source: Further, the benefits of vaccination in the passive phase are less than the active, and 2–5-year-old vaccinees show a greatly increased risk of hospitalisation than controls.
evidence: This is an observation from the trial data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 2–5-year-old vaccinees show a greatly increased risk of hospitalisation than controls in the passive phase.
source: Further, the benefits of vaccination in the passive phase are less than the active, and 2–5-year-old vaccinees show a greatly increased risk of hospitalisation than controls.
evidence: This is an observation from the trial data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In both trials, a mix of infecting serotypes among cases was observed.
source: In both trials, a mix of infecting serotypes among cases was observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the trial data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The vaccine has the greatest benefit for seropositive recipients.
source: The vaccine has the greatest benefit for seropositive recipients: hazard ratios remain low throughout the active phase and the first year of passive phase, and mean posterior and 95% credible intervals are below 1 for all ages, indicating consistent benefit.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For seropositive recipients, hazard ratios remain low throughout the active phase and the first year of passive phase.
source: The vaccine has the greatest benefit for seropositive recipients: hazard ratios remain low throughout the active phase and the first year of passive phase, and mean posterior and 95% credible intervals are below 1 for all ages, indicating consistent benefit.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For seropositive recipients, mean posterior and 95% credible intervals of hazard ratios are below 1 for all ages, indicating consistent benefit.
source: The vaccine has the greatest benefit for seropositive recipients: hazard ratios remain low throughout the active phase and the first year of passive phase, and mean posterior and 95% credible intervals are below 1 for all ages, indicating consistent benefit.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decrease in hazard ratios over time in each age group reflects the greater benefit to seropositives against hospitalised/severe disease.
source: The decrease in hazard ratios over time in each age group reflects the greater benefit to seropositives against hospitalised/severe disease as only this disease outcome is measured in the passive phase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: For seronegative vaccinees, hazard ratios are neither significantly positive nor negative during the first year.
source: For seronegative vaccinees, hazard ratios are neither significantly positive nor negative during the first year.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For seronegative vaccinees, hazard ratios rise dramatically after the first year.
source: Ratios rise dramatically afterwards, reflecting low and short-lived immunity, combined with an almost sixfold long-term increase in disease risk, in both trials and in all age groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For seronegative vaccinees, there is an almost sixfold long-term increase in disease risk.
source: Ratios rise dramatically afterwards, reflecting low and short-lived immunity, combined with an almost sixfold long-term increase in disease risk, in both trials and in all age groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increase in hazard ratios for seronegatives in the passive phase refers to an increase in risk of hospitalisation.
source: Because the passive phase trial surveillance detected only hospitalised disease, this increase in hazard ratios refers to an increase in risk of hospitalisation, consistent with the 2017 NS1 data (Sridhar et al., 2018), to which our model was not fitted.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of trial design, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The modeling results are consistent with the 2017 NS1 data.
source: Because the passive phase trial surveillance detected only hospitalised disease, this increase in hazard ratios refers to an increase in risk of hospitalisation, consistent with the 2017 NS1 data (Sridhar et al., 2018), to which our model was not fitted.
evidence: This is a comparison of the modeling results with independent published data.

claim: The model was not fitted to the 2017 NS1 data.
source: Because the passive phase trial surveillance detected only hospitalised disease, this increase in hazard ratios refers to an increase in risk of hospitalisation, consistent with the 2017 NS1 data (Sridhar et al., 2018), to which our model was not fitted.
evidence: This clarifies the independence of the model validation.

claim: When unstratified by baseline serostatus, the vaccine is broadly beneficial.
source: When unstratified by baseline serostatus, the vaccine is broadly beneficial, although hazard ratios rise over time, and are above 1 for 2–5 year olds in the first year of passive follow up.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: When unstratified by baseline serostatus, hazard ratios rise over time.
source: When unstratified by baseline serostatus, the vaccine is broadly beneficial, although hazard ratios rise over time, and are above 1 for 2–5 year olds in the first year of passive follow up.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: When unstratified by baseline serostatus, hazard ratios are above 1 for 2–5 year olds in the first year of passive follow up.
source: When unstratified by baseline serostatus, the vaccine is broadly beneficial, although hazard ratios rise over time, and are above 1 for 2–5 year olds in the first year of passive follow up.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Decreasing hazard ratios with age reflect increasing seropositivity with age.
source: Decreasing hazard ratios with age reflect increasing seropositivity with age, and to a lesser extent the increase with age in transient immunity that we infer for seropositives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Decreasing hazard ratios with age reflect the increase with age in transient immunity inferred for seropositives.
source: Decreasing hazard ratios with age reflect increasing seropositivity with age, and to a lesser extent the increase with age in transient immunity that we infer for seropositives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Low seroprevalence in 2–5 year olds is the driving factor of their increased risk.
source: Low seroprevalence in 2–5 year olds is the driving factor of their increased risk, and this is consistent with the risk enhancement observed in the first year of long-term follow-up data.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increased risk in 2–5 year olds is consistent with the risk enhancement observed in the first year of long-term follow-up data.
source: Low seroprevalence in 2–5 year olds is the driving factor of their increased risk, and this is consistent with the risk enhancement observed in the first year of long-term follow-up data.
evidence: This is a comparison of the modeling results with observed trial data.

claim: Hazard ratios are similar between trials for comparable age groups.
source: Hazard ratios are similar between trials for comparable age groups.

claim: Vaccination offers the greatest benefit to serotype 4.

claim: For serotypes 3 and 4, hazard ratios are lower.
source: For serotypes 3 and 4, hazard ratios are lower, and vaccination provides some initial protection even in seronegatives, although again these ratios rise over time.

claim: For serotypes 3 and 4, vaccination provides some initial protection even in seronegatives.
source: For serotypes 3 and 4, hazard ratios are lower, and vaccination provides some initial protection even in seronegatives, although again these ratios rise over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Risk enhancement of 2–5-year-old vaccinees is much higher for serotypes 1 and 2 than for 3 and 4.
source: Risk enhancement of 2–5-year-old vaccinees is much higher for serotypes 1 and 2 than for 3 and 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among unvaccinated individuals, primary infection is 70% as likely to cause symptomatic disease as secondary infection (relative risk 0.7, 95% CI 0.36–0.98).
source: We estimate the relative risk parameters K0,0 and K2,0 to be 0.7 (0.36–0.98) and 0.31 (0.14–0.63), respectively. That is, among unvaccinated individuals, primary infection is 70% as likely, and tertiary/quaternary infection is 31% as likely, to cause symptomatic disease as secondary infection.
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Among unvaccinated individuals, tertiary/quaternary infection is 31% as likely to cause symptomatic disease as secondary infection (relative risk 0.31, 95% CI 0.14–0.63).
source: We estimate the relative risk parameters K0,0 and K2,0 to be 0.7 (0.36–0.98) and 0.31 (0.14–0.63), respectively. That is, among unvaccinated individuals, primary infection is 70% as likely, and tertiary/quaternary infection is 31% as likely, to cause symptomatic disease as secondary infection.
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Seronegative vaccinees increase their long-term risk of symptomatic disease by a factor of 1.5 (1.0–2.7).

evidence: This is a derived estimate from the modeling analysis based on parameter values in Table 1.

claim: Vaccinees with a single prior infection multiply their long-term disease risk by a factor of 0.31 (0.14–0.63).
source: However, considering vaccination as a silent infection, seronegative vaccinees increase their long-term risk of symptomatic disease by a factor of K1,0/K0,0 = 1.5 (1.0–2.7), whereas vaccinees with a single prior infection multiply their long-term disease risk by a factor of K2,0/K1,0 = 0.31 (0.14–0.63), transient immunity notwithstanding.
evidence: This is a derived estimate from the modeling analysis based on parameter values in Table 1.

evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: In seronegatives, vaccination increases long-term risk of hospitalisation by a factor of 6.1 (4.1–11).
source: Therefore, in seronegatives, vaccination increases long-term risk of hospitalisation by a factor of K1,0 K1,1/K0,0 K0,1 = 6.1 (4.1–11), whereas for those with a single prior infection hospitalisation risk is multiplied by a factor of K2,0 K2,1/K1,0 K1,1 = 0.078 (0.036–0.16), again without considering transient immunity.
evidence: This is a derived estimate from the modeling analysis based on parameter values in Table 1.

claim: For those with a single prior infection, vaccination multiplies hospitalisation risk by a factor of 0.078 (0.036–0.16).
source: Therefore, in seronegatives, vaccination increases long-term risk of hospitalisation by a factor of K1,0 K1,1/K0,0 K0,1 = 6.1 (4.1–11), whereas for those with a single prior infection hospitalisation risk is multiplied by a factor of K2,0 K2,1/K1,0 K1,1 = 0.078 (0.036–0.16), again without considering transient immunity.
evidence: This is a derived estimate from the modeling analysis based on parameter values in Table 1.

claim: For every serotype, seronegative transient immunity estimates do not vary for older age groups but are lower for 2–5 year olds.
source: For every serotype, seronegative transient immunity estimates do not vary for older age groups but are lower for 2–5 year olds.

claim: Seronegative transient immunity estimates are lowest for serotype 2 (with negative mean estimates of −11% (−72–46%) for 2–5 year olds).
source: They are lowest for serotype 2 (with negative mean estimates of −11% (−72–46%) for 2–5 year olds) and relatively high for serotypes 3 and 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Seronegative transient immunity estimates are relatively high for serotypes 3 and 4.
source: They are lowest for serotype 2 (with negative mean estimates of −11% (−72–46%) for 2–5 year olds) and relatively high for serotypes 3 and 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: For seropositives, transient immunity estimates vary less by serotype but more by age.
source: For seropositives, while estimates are again higher for serotypes 3 and 4, they vary less by serotype but more by age, with immunity being lower for younger than older children.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: For seropositives, immunity is lower for younger than older children.
source: For seropositives, while estimates are again higher for serotypes 3 and 4, they vary less by serotype but more by age, with immunity being lower for younger than older children.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Transient immunity varies by age, independently of serostatus.
source: Our results imply that transient immunity varies by age, independently of serostatus, although more so in seropositives (Figure 5, Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Transient immunity varies more by age in seropositives than in seronegatives.
source: Our results imply that transient immunity varies by age, independently of serostatus, although more so in seropositives (Figure 5, Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Mean posterior estimates of seronegative transient immunity duration are 4.5 (1–9.6) years.
source: Mean posterior estimates of seronegative and seropositive transient immunity duration are 4.5 (1–9.6) and 11 (2.3–20) years, respectively.
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Mean posterior estimates of seropositive transient immunity duration are 11 (2.3–20) years.
source: Mean posterior estimates of seronegative and seropositive transient immunity duration are 4.5 (1–9.6) and 11 (2.3–20) years, respectively.
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: In seropositives, approximately equal weight is given to longer durations of between 5 and 20 years (85% of posterior mass is above 5 years).
source: However, a closer look at parameter posterior distributions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, top row) is informative: in seropositives, approximately equal weight is given to longer durations of between 5 and 20 years (85% of posterior mass is above 5 years), whereas in seronegatives shorter durations are more likely (modal estimate is approximately 2 years and 62% of posterior mass is below 5 years).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In seronegatives, shorter durations of transient immunity are more likely (modal estimate is approximately 2 years and 62% of posterior mass is below 5 years).
source: However, a closer look at parameter posterior distributions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, top row) is informative: in seropositives, approximately equal weight is given to longer durations of between 5 and 20 years (85% of posterior mass is above 5 years), whereas in seronegatives shorter durations are more likely (modal estimate is approximately 2 years and 62% of posterior mass is below 5 years).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Model fits that fix seropositive transient immunity at zero do not reproduce the trial data.
source: If seropositive transient immunity were zero (or alternatively if the duration of transient immunity in seropositives was very short), then vaccination would only prime immunity and only individuals with pre-existing monotypic immunity would benefit from vaccination. Instead we estimate positive values for transient immunity for each age group and serotype. Further, model fits that fix seropositive transient immunity at zero do not reproduce the trial data.
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: For seropositives, to the extent that transient immunity is long-lived, vaccination confers benefit beyond that of priming immunity and consequent reduction of disease risk to that associated with natural tertiary and quaternary infection.
source: Therefore, for seropositives, to the extent that transient immunity is long-lived, vaccination confers benefit beyond that of priming immunity and consequent reduction of disease risk to that associated with natural tertiary and quaternary infection.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Individuals with pre-existing multitypic immunity are predicted to benefit from vaccination.
source: Hence individuals with pre-existing multitypic immunity are also predicted to benefit from vaccination, with the caveat that we were not able to test a model in which transient immunity only applied to those with monotypic immunity.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis with a stated limitation.

claim: In seronegatives, any positive benefit that mitigates long-term increase in disease risk is short-lived.
source: Conversely, in seronegatives, any positive benefit that mitigates long-term increase in disease risk is short-lived.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: The age group-specific multiplier of the baseline hazard increases with age for 6–11 year olds (1.2, 0.91–1.5).
source: We find that the age group-specific multiplier of the baseline hazard increases with age for 6–11 year olds (1.2, 0.91–1.5), but then decreases for the 12–16 age group (1.1, 0.79–1.5) to be no different from the 2–5-year-old age group in the mean posterior estimates.
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The age group-specific multiplier of the baseline hazard decreases for the 12–16 age group (1.1, 0.79–1.5) to be no different from the 2–5-year-old age group in the mean posterior estimates.
source: We find that the age group-specific multiplier of the baseline hazard increases with age for 6–11 year olds (1.2, 0.91–1.5), but then decreases for the 12–16 age group (1.1, 0.79–1.5) to be no different from the 2–5-year-old age group in the mean posterior estimates.
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Model runs that omit the age-specific hazard multiplier give a noticeably inferior visual fit.
source: While both credible intervals encompass 1 (indicating no difference), model runs that omit this age-specific hazard multiplier give a noticeably inferior visual fit (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: Seropositives are 0.77 (0.43–0.99) times as likely to be infected as seronegatives due to their immunity to at least one serotype.
